title: 2  Reproducible writing
text:
2.1 A familiar handoff
Reproducible writing is the practice of keeping claims, calculations, figures, tables, and their sources connected closely enough that the document can be rebuilt and checked. Quarto provides the machinery; good project habits make the machinery portable.
Most researchers have either received a project like this or created one under deadline pressure. Reproducible writing tries to make the handoff instead:
That is a much smaller and testable process.

title: 2  Reproducible writing
text:
“It works on my computer”
A colleague sends you a folder called final_analysis_revised_3. Their email says:

Open analysis.R, change the first setwd() line to wherever you saved the folder, run lines 1–287, ignore the warnings, then open paper.docx. Figure 2 should match the plot in the figures-old folder, except the number in the Results section was updated manually.

Before checking the research, you must reconstruct the colleague’s computer: their folders, execution order, interactive objects, package versions, and copy-and-paste history. Even if every statistical command is correct, the handoff is fragile.


1. Open the project folder.
2. Install the documented requirements.
3. Render manuscript.qmd.
4. Inspect the source, output, and any reported differences.

title: 2  Reproducible writing
text:
2.2 Source, process, and output
Literate programming places human explanation and executable instructions in one source document (Knuth 1984). Quarto coordinates the rendering process:
source data + .qmd + software environment
                    |
                 render
                    |
          HTML / PDF / Word / slides / tutorials
The rendered PDF is not the reproducible object by itself. It is evidence that a particular source was rendered in a particular environment. The useful object to share is the project that can recreate it.
This changes the role of common files:








File
Role
Usually edited by




data/training-study.csv
Input
Data producer or documented cleaning step


manuscript.qmd
Narrative and analysis instructions
Author


bibliography.bib
Citation metadata
Author/reference manager


manuscript.html
Rendered product
Quarto


manuscript.pdf
Rendered product
Quarto and LaTeX



If a rendered product looks wrong, repair the source or process and render again. Editing the product directly creates an undocumented fork.

title: 2  Reproducible writing
text:
2.3 Why absolute paths fail
An absolute path starts from a computer-specific root:
# macOS
readr::read_csv("/Users/alex/Desktop/project/data/results.csv")

# Windows
readr::read_csv("C:/Users/alex/OneDrive - University/project/data/results.csv")

# Linux or a research server
readr::read_csv("/home/alex/projects/project/data/results.csv")
The path may be correct today, but it encodes facts that are not properties of the research:

the operating system;
the author’s username;
the name of a university or cloud-storage service;
where the author happened to save the project;
which drive or network mount was available; and
sometimes confidential project, client, or participant names.

When someone else receives the project, at least one of those facts changes. The code fails before it reaches the analysis.

2.3.1 The same author can still break it
Absolute paths are not only a collaboration problem. They fail when you:

move the project from Downloads to Documents;
rename a parent folder;
switch from a desktop to a laptop;
restore from a backup;
run on a high-performance computer;
change institutions or cloud-storage accounts; or
ask an automated build service to render the document.

An absolute path is therefore a claim that this project will always live in this exact location on this exact kind of machine.


2.3.2 setwd() moves the problem
A common repair is:
setwd("/Users/alex/Desktop/project")
The remaining paths may now look relative, but every collaborator still has to edit the script before it can run. Worse, setwd() changes global session state: later code depends on whether that line ran and what the working directory was beforehand.
Opening a project establishes one shared root without hard-coding each user’s computer.


2.3.3 Relative paths are the solution
Inside the workshop project, write:
readr::read_csv("data/training-study.csv")
This path means:

start from the project root;
enter the data folder; and
open training-study.csv.

It describes the relationship between files, which remains true when the whole project is moved.







Path
Meaning




data/file.csv
A file below the project root


figures/result.png
A generated or supplied figure folder


scripts/clean.R
A script below the root


../shared/file.csv
A file outside the project — portable only if that surrounding structure is also shared


/data/file.csv
An absolute path from the filesystem root, not the project









WarningRelative does not mean “any path without a username”



../someone-elses-folder/data.csv is syntactically relative but still depends on a directory outside the shared project. Prefer keeping shareable inputs inside the project, or document and validate the external data location explicitly.

title: 2  Reproducible writing
text:
2.4 The project root
Your editor and Quarto need a stable answer to “relative to what?” For this workshop, the extracted folder containing _quarto.yml is the project root:
quarto-workshop-starter/
├── _quarto.yml
├── manuscript.qmd
├── bibliography.bib
├── data/
│   ├── training-study.csv
│   └── README.md
└── _extensions/
Open the folder, not just an isolated .qmd file. Run terminal commands from that folder. Quarto then has a consistent base for documents and resources.
You can see R’s current working directory with:
getwd()
Use this for diagnosis, not as a value to copy into setwd().

title: 2  Reproducible writing
text:
2.5 Separate inputs from products
A project becomes easier to understand when its folders communicate intent:
project/
├── data/          # original or documented inputs
├── R/             # reusable functions, if the project grows
├── figures/       # supplied figures; generated figures may be temporary
├── manuscript.qmd # source
├── bibliography.bib
└── README.md      # how to reproduce the project
Useful rules are:

do not overwrite raw inputs during analysis;
derive cleaned variables in code;
give files stable, descriptive names;
keep secrets and confidential data out of distributable projects;
avoid folders named only old, new, final, or misc; and
make it obvious which files are sources and which are generated.

title: 2  Reproducible writing
text:
2.6 Four layers of reproducibility
Keeping data and code together is necessary but not sufficient.

2.6.1 1. Computational
Can the recorded instructions recreate the values, figures, and tables?
Common failures include missing code, interactive objects, manual spreadsheet edits, and undocumented execution order.


2.6.2 2. Environmental
Can the instructions run with the available versions of R, packages, Quarto, LaTeX, and system libraries?
The workshop records sessionInfo(). Package lockfiles such as renv provide a stronger environment specification.


2.6.3 3. Provenance
Can a reader identify where data and external information came from, what was changed, and under what permissions?
A mysterious final.csv is not made trustworthy merely by reading it with reproducible code.


2.6.4 4. Narrative
Do the prose, captions, and conclusions accurately describe the computations?
Code can keep n = 40 synchronised with a dataset. It cannot decide whether a causal claim is justified. Reproducibility makes reasoning inspectable; it does not replace judgement.

title: 2  Reproducible writing
text:
2.7 Clean sessions expose hidden dependencies
Suppose you created study_clean interactively yesterday, then wrote:
mean(study_clean$change)
The line works while that object remains in your Global Environment. It fails on a colleague’s computer because the document never creates study_clean.
A clean render starts a new execution context and runs the document in order. This exposes:

missing package calls;
objects created only interactively;
files read from the wrong location;
dependence on a particular execution order; and
values copied rather than calculated.

The failure is useful evidence about what the source has not yet documented.

title: 2  Reproducible writing
text:
2.8 A practical handoff contract
Before sharing a project, ask whether a colleague can answer:

Which file should I open first?
Where are the inputs, and may they be shared?
Which command recreates the outputs?
Which software and packages are required?
Which files should never be edited manually?
What result should I see if the render succeeds?

The workshop’s README.md, setup.R, preflight.R, and .qmd sources provide those answers at a modest level. More complex projects may add a package lockfile, tests, workflow manager, or container.

title: 2  Reproducible writing
text:
2.9 Try the handoff yourself
Open manuscript.qmd and data/training-study.csv.

Find the code that reads the CSV.
Confirm that the path contains no username or drive letter.
Move a copy of the entire project folder to a different location.
Open the copied folder as a project and render the manuscript.
Move only manuscript.qmd without its project and observe what is missing.
Explain why the first move succeeds and the second is not a complete handoff.


2.9.1 Checkpoint
You should be able to describe the project as a self-contained set of relationships between files—not as a folder that happens to work from one person’s Desktop.

In Chapter 3 we turn the narrative itself into structured, portable source. In Chapter 4 we make calculated values and outputs part of the same rendering process.




Knuth, Donald E. 1984. “Literate Programming.” The Computer Journal 27 (2): 97–111. https://doi.org/10.1093/comjnl/27.2.97.

title: 3  Writing in Markdown
text:
3.1 Source versus appearance
Markdown is plain text with punctuation that describes structure rather than appearance. You identify something as a heading, quotation, citation, or code expression; the output format decides how that structure should look.
That separation is what allows the same source to become a web page, PDF, Word document, book chapter, slide deck, or tutorial.
In a word processor, “make this 18-point bold” is a visual instruction. In Markdown, ## Methods says “this is a second-level heading.” Quarto can then:
Semantic structure is both more reusable and more accessible than manual visual formatting.

title: 3  Writing in Markdown
3  Writing in Markdown
text:
3.2 Document metadata
A Quarto document begins with YAML metadata between --- lines:
---
title: "A reproducible analysis"
subtitle: "A synthetic training study"
author: "A. Researcher"
date: today
bibliography: bibliography.bib
format:
  html:
    toc: true
  pdf:
    number-sections: true
---
The YAML is configuration. It answers questions such as:

What is the document called?
Who wrote it?
Which bibliography should be used?
Which outputs should be created?
Which options differ between those outputs?

Indentation defines nesting:
format:
  html:             # belongs under format
    toc: true       # belongs under html
  pdf:              # also belongs under format
    number-sections: true
If toc were aligned with format, it would have a different scope.

title: 3  Writing in Markdown
text:
3.3 Headings create document structure
Use one # for a level-one heading, two for level two, and so on:


Source
# Introduction

## Background

## Research question

# Methods

## Data

## Analysis


Rendered structure
1 Introduction
  1.1 Background
  1.2 Research question
2 Methods
  2.1 Data
  2.2 Analysis
The precise numbering and typography come from the output format.


Do not skip from # to ### simply because you prefer the smaller font. That creates a broken outline for navigation and assistive technology. Change the theme if the visual design needs adjustment (more on this later).

title: 3  Writing in Markdown
text:
3.4 Section numbering and cross-references
Turn on numbering for an output:
format:
  html:
    number-sections: true
  pdf:
    number-sections: true
Give a heading a stable identifier:
## Statistical analysis {#sec-statistical-analysis}
Refer to it with:
The model specification is described in @sec-statistical-analysis.
Quarto writes “Section 3.2” or the appropriate number. If the section moves, the reference updates automatically.


Source
## Data preparation {#sec-data-preparation}

Missing values were retained for descriptive checks.

## Statistical analysis

See @sec-data-preparation before fitting the model.


Rendered idea

3.1 Data preparation
Missing values were retained for descriptive checks.
3.2 Statistical analysis
See Section 3.1 before fitting the model.



Stable identifiers are better than writing “see the section above” or manually typing “Section 3.1”. Use short, descriptive, lowercase labels separated by hyphens.
Quarto uses the same system for sections, figures, tables, equations, listings, and exercises:



Object
Label prefix
Reference




Section
sec-
@sec-methods


Figure
fig-
@fig-change


Table
tbl-
@tbl-summary


Equation
eq-
@eq-change


Listing
lst-
@lst-model

title: 3  Writing in Markdown
text:
3.5 Paragraphs and emphasis
A blank line starts a new paragraph. A single line break in the source normally continues the same paragraph, allowing you to wrap source text without changing the rendered prose.


Source
This is one paragraph even though the
source wraps across two lines.

This is a new paragraph with *emphasis*,
**strong emphasis**, and `inline code`.


Rendered
This is one paragraph even though the source wraps across two lines.
This is a new paragraph with emphasis, strong emphasis, and inline code.


Use emphasis to convey meaning, not to simulate headings. Backticks are useful for filenames, functions, variables, and short commands.

title: 3  Writing in Markdown
text:
3.6 Lists
Unordered lists use -; ordered lists use 1.. Markdown can number ordered lists automatically:


Source
The analysis will:

- read the source data;
- derive the change score; and
- produce a figure.

The reader should:

1. open the project;
1. render the manuscript;
1. inspect the output.


Rendered
The analysis will:

read the source data;
derive the change score; and
produce a figure.

The reader should:

open the project;
render the manuscript;
inspect the output.



Using 1. for every ordered item makes rearranging source easier. Use explicit numbers only when the source number itself matters.

title: 3  Writing in Markdown
text:
3.7 Links, images, and footnotes
[Quarto documentation](https://quarto.org/docs/guide/)

![A concise description of the image](images/result.png)

This claim needs a qualification.[^qualification]

[^qualification]: The data are synthetic and illustrate workflow only.
Good link text tells the reader where the link goes. Avoid “click here”.
Image text inside ![...] becomes alternative text. Describe the information a reader needs, not merely the filename or “image of a graph”.
Footnotes are appropriate for supplementary explanation. If information is central to interpreting the result, keep it in the main text.

title: 3  Writing in Markdown
text:
3.8 Quotations and block quotes
Prefix quoted paragraphs with >:


Source
> Reproducibility is a property of a
> workflow, not simply a file format.


Rendered

Reproducibility is a property of a workflow, not simply a file format.



For published words, include a citation and page or section locator where appropriate. Markdown syntax does not remove scholarly attribution requirements.

title: 3  Writing in Markdown
text:
3.9 Callouts
Callouts separate warnings, definitions, tips, or assumptions from the main narrative:
::: {.callout-warning}
The data are synthetic and must not be interpreted as evidence.
:::






Warning



The data are synthetic and must not be interpreted as evidence.


Common types are note, tip, important, warning, and caution. A callout should add meaning, not turn every paragraph into a coloured box.

title: 3  Writing in Markdown
text:
3.10 Tables written in Markdown
Small, static tables can be written directly:


Source
| Format | Best suited to |
|---|---|
| HTML | Browsing and interaction |
| PDF | Fixed-page distribution |
| DOCX | Editorial workflows |


Rendered



Format
Best suited to




HTML
Browsing and interaction


PDF
Fixed-page distribution


DOCX
Editorial workflows





Use a code-generated table when values come from data. A hand-written Markdown table is appropriate for stable explanatory content such as option summaries.

title: 3  Writing in Markdown
text:
3.11 Mathematics and numbered equations
Inline mathematics uses one pair of dollar signs:
The individual change is $\Delta_i = y_{i1} - y_{i0}$.
The rendered result is: the individual change is Δi=yi1−yi0\Delta_i = y_{i1} - y_{i0}.
A display equation uses $$. Add a label inside braces for numbering and cross-referencing:
$$
\bar{\Delta}_g =
\frac{1}{n_g}\sum_{i=1}^{n_g}\Delta_i
$$ {#eq-group-change}

Group means are defined in @eq-group-change.
Δ‾g=1ng∑i=1ngΔi(3.1)
\bar{\Delta}_g =
\frac{1}{n_g}\sum_{i=1}^{n_g}\Delta_i
 \qquad(3.1)
Group means are defined in Equation 3.1.

title: 3  Writing in Markdown
text:
3.12 Citations and bibliographies
Bibliographic records live in bibliography.bib. A record has a citation key:
@article{knuth1984,
  author = {Knuth, Donald E.},
  title = {Literate Programming},
  year = {1984}
}
Use the key in prose:


Source
Literate programming was formalised by
@knuth1984.

Reproducibility requires more than
retaining code [@sandve2013].


Rendered
Literate programming was formalised by Knuth (1984).
Reproducibility requires more than retaining code (Sandve et al. 2013).


Quarto formats the citation and builds the reference list. A Citation Style Language (.csl) file can change the style without rewriting citations.
Useful citation patterns include:
[@knuth1984]                 # parenthetical
@knuth1984                  # textual author
[@knuth1984, pp. 100–102]   # locator
[@knuth1984; @sandve2013]   # multiple sources
The bibliography automates formatting, not source evaluation. Check names, titles, dates, identifiers, and whether the cited source supports the claim.
Probably the easiest way to get bib keys is from Zotero and the Better BibTeX extension which can export the required format for a .bib file automatically.

title: 3  Writing in Markdown
text:
3.13 A fuller Markdown exercise
In manuscript.qmd:

Complete the title, subtitle, author, and output options in YAML.
Create Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion, and References sections.
Add stable sec- identifiers to Methods and Results.
Refer to Methods from the Results prose.
Add a research question, bulleted aims, and the numbered change-score equation.
Add one citation, one footnote, one link, and one warning callout.
Render to HTML and inspect the table of contents, numbering, and references.
Render to PDF and identify what changed visually and what remained semantically the same.


3.13.1 Checkpoint
The source contains structure rather than manual styling. Headings appear in navigation, section and equation references update automatically, and citations are generated from the bibliography.

Chapter 4 applies the same source-to-output principle to calculated values, figures, and tables.




Knuth, Donald E. 1984. “Literate Programming.” The Computer Journal 27 (2): 97–111. https://doi.org/10.1093/comjnl/27.2.97.


Sandve, Geir Kjetil, Anton Nekrutenko, James Taylor, and Eivind Hovig. 2013. “Ten Simple Rules for Reproducible Computational Research.” PLOS Computational Biology 9 (10): e1003285. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003285.

title: 4  Literate computation
text:
4.1 Anatomy of an R cell
An executable document contains three interleaved kinds of material:
The rendered document is a record of code executed in context, not a screenshot of an interactive session.
An executable R cell begins with ```{r} and ends with three backticks. Cell options sit at the top and begin with #|:
When this book renders, that pattern produces a live demonstration:
study |>
  count(group)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  group            n
  <chr>        <int>
1 comparison      20
2 intervention    20
The cell has:
Labels should be unique, descriptive, and stable. Labels with reserved prefixes such as fig- and tbl- create cross-referenceable outputs.

title: 4  Literate computation
4  Literate computation
text:
4.2 The execution model
For an R-based .qmd, Quarto asks knitr to execute cells from top to bottom. Objects created in an earlier cell are available later in that render.
# Cell 1
study <- readr::read_csv("data/training-study.csv")

# Cell 2: depends on Cell 1
nrow(study)
This has several consequences:

changing cell order can change whether code works;
a document should create every object it uses;
packages should be loaded or namespaced in the source;
interactive Global Environment objects are not reliable dependencies; and
restarting R before rendering is a useful test.


4.2.1 A common hidden-state failure
Imagine running this interactively:
study_with_change <- study |>
  mutate(change = followup_score - baseline_score)
You then write a document cell containing only:
mean(study_with_change$change)
It works until R is restarted. The document contains the result-producing line but not the instruction that creates its input. A clean render reveals the missing step.

title: 4  Literate computation
section: 4.3 Cell options control execution and presentation
text:
4.3 Cell options control execution and presentation
Chunk options are not cosmetic trivia. They determine what runs, what readers see, what can be referenced, and how output is presented.

4.3.1 Core execution and visibility options










Option
Typical value
Code runs?
Code shown?
Output shown?




eval
false
No
Yes
No


echo
false
Yes
No
Yes


output
false
Yes
Yes
No


include
false
Yes
No
No


warning
false
Yes
As configured
Warnings hidden


message
false
Yes
As configured
Messages hidden


error
true
Yes
As configured
Error displayed; render continues



These options answer different questions:

Should the code run? eval
Should readers see the code? echo
Should readers see its normal output? output
Should anything from the cell appear? include
How should diagnostics be handled? warning, message, error



4.3.2 Default: code and output
Use the default when the calculation itself is part of the explanation:

study |>
  summarise(
    participants = n(),
    mean_change = mean(change)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  participants mean_change
         <int>       <dbl>
1           40        6.95


The reader can inspect the instructions and the result.


4.3.3 echo: false: show the result, hide the implementation
This is common in a polished reader-facing report:


# A tibble: 2 × 2
  group            n
  <chr>        <int>
1 comparison      20
2 intervention    20


The code still runs and remains in the .qmd source, but the rendered reader sees only the result. Hiding code is a presentation choice, not reproducibility by itself; the source must still be available to someone expected to audit it.


4.3.4 eval: false: show an example without running it

# An illustrative call that should not run during this render
download.file("https://example.org/large-data.csv", "data/large-data.csv")

This is useful for teaching installation commands, destructive examples, slow jobs, or code requiring credentials. Do not use it for code that supposedly created the reported result.


4.3.5 output: false: run code, hide normal output

summary_table <- study |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(mean_change = mean(change), .groups = "drop")

summary_table

The object is created for later cells, and the code is visible, but the printed table is suppressed here.


4.3.6 include: false: setup that remains out of the document
The first cell in this chapter loaded packages and data using:
#| include: false

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
study <- read_csv("materials/complete/data/training-study.csv")
The code ran, but neither code nor output appeared. This is appropriate for routine setup. It is not a place to conceal analytically important decisions.


4.3.7 Warnings and messages
Package startup messages rarely help a manuscript reader:
#| message: false
#| warning: false
Suppress expected noise only after understanding it. A convergence warning, failed transformation, or removed observation may be evidence of an analysis problem. Fix or explain substantive warnings rather than hiding them globally.


4.3.8 Folding rather than removing code
HTML can keep code available without placing it in the main reading flow:
format:
  html:
    code-fold: true
    code-summary: "Show the R code"
This affects HTML interaction. PDF cannot fold code, so decide separately whether code should be shown, hidden, or moved to an appendix.

title: 4  Literate computation
text:
4.4 Where options can be set
Options can apply at three levels.

4.4.1 Project level
In _quarto.yml:
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
Use project defaults for consistent policy across documents.


4.4.2 Document level
In a document’s YAML:
---
execute:
  echo: true
  warning: false
---
Use document defaults for the intended audience of that document.


4.4.3 Cell level
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
Cell options override broader defaults for one case. The practical precedence is:
project default < document default < cell option
Keep exceptions local and intentional. If every cell repeats the same option, move it to document or project YAML.

title: 4  Literate computation
text:
4.5 Inline computation
Inline code places a calculated value inside a sentence. The source pattern is:
The study contains `r nrow(study)` participants.
In this rendered chapter, the live sentence is:

The study contains 40 participants.

Other source examples include:

The mean change was `r round(mean(study$change), 1)` points.
There were `r dplyr::n_distinct(study$group)` study groups.

Use short, readable expressions inline. If a calculation is complicated, create a clearly named object in a cell and insert only that object:
overall_mean_change <- mean(study$change)
The prose can then use:
The mean change was `r round(overall_mean_change, 1)` points.
This keeps prose readable and makes the calculation easier to test.

title: 4  Literate computation
text:
4.6 Figures, options, and cross-references
A figure cell combines execution options with publication metadata:
#| label: fig-change-demo
#| fig-cap: "Change score by training hours and study group."
#| fig-alt: "Scatterplot of training hours against change score..."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| dpi: 300

ggplot(study, aes(training_hours, change, colour = group, shape = group)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)
The live output is Figure 4.1:

ggplot(study, aes(training_hours, change, colour = group, shape = group)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    x = "Training hours",
    y = "Change in score",
    colour = "Study group",
    shape = "Study group"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'








Figure 4.1: Change score by training hours and study group.





Important figure options include:



Option
Purpose




label: fig-name
Creates a stable cross-reference target


fig-cap
Visible caption


fig-alt
Accessible description of information in the figure


fig-width, fig-height
Size of the plotting device in inches


dpi
Raster resolution


fig-align
Alignment in the output


fig-show: hold
Holds multiple plots from one cell together



Plot dimensions affect the space in which the plot is drawn, not merely how a finished image is stretched. Text, facets, and legends may reflow when dimensions change.

title: 4  Literate computation
text:
4.7 Tables and cross-references
Create the data object in code:
Then present it with a caption and table label:

knitr::kable(group_summary, digits = 1)



Table 4.1: Change scores by study group.






group

Table 4.1 is numbered and referenced from prose. If another table is inserted earlier, Quarto updates the number.
Keep a distinction between:

the data object (group_summary);
the presentation function (knitr::kable()); and
the interpretation in prose.

This makes it easier to change table styling without recalculating the result.

title: 4  Literate computation
text:
4.8 Results produced “as is”
Some R functions deliberately return Markdown or HTML. With knitr, results: 'asis' or Quarto’s output: asis can ask the renderer to interpret returned markup rather than print it literally.
Use this only when the code is intentionally generating document structure. Untrusted text must not be inserted as raw HTML, and format-specific markup may fail in PDF or Word.

title: 4  Literate computation
text:
4.9 Errors during rendering
By default, an error stops the render. This is usually correct: a document with a failed analysis should not silently produce a polished output.
For a teaching document that intentionally demonstrates an error:
#| error: true

mean("not numeric")
The error appears in the rendered lesson and the document continues. Do not set error: true globally in a production manuscript merely to obtain an output.

title: 4  Literate computation
text:
4.10 Randomness
Simulations, sampling, model initialisation, and some algorithms use random numbers. Without a seed, repeated renders may differ:
set.seed(20260729)
sample(1:100, 5)
A seed makes the pseudorandom sequence repeatable. It does not make a simulation design appropriate or guarantee identical results across every software implementation.

title: 4  Literate computation
text:
4.11 Caching and freezing
Two related features can avoid unnecessary computation:

cell caching can reuse a cell’s previous computational result; and
Quarto freeze can reuse rendered computational Markdown for a document.

Examples:
execute:
  cache: true
execute:
  freeze: auto
These improve rendering speed, but cached output can conceal missing external dependencies during testing. Before release, perform at least one clean, uncached render in a fresh copy or controlled environment.
Never use caching as a substitute for recording inputs.

title: 4  Literate computation
text:
4.12 Choosing options for the reader
The same analysis can be presented differently:







Audience
Reasonable presentation




Analyst collaborator
Show code and output


Journal reader
Hide routine setup; show methods-critical code selectively


Auditor or reviewer
Provide source or folded code plus environment details


Student
Show starter code; reserve answers for solution output


Lecture audience
Hide most code and enlarge the explanatory figure



Chunk options let one computational workflow support these audiences, but a document should not pretend that hidden source does not exist.

title: 4  Literate computation
text:
4.13 A substantial computation exercise
In manuscript.qmd:

Add an include: false setup cell that loads packages and reads the CSV.
Derive change in code.
Replace typed sample-size and group-count values with inline R.
Create a summary object in a hidden setup cell.
Present it in a tbl- cell with a caption and refer to it from prose.
Create a fig- cell with a caption, informative alt text, explicit dimensions, and both colour and shape mappings.
Use code-fold for HTML and decide explicitly how code appears in PDF.
Restart R and render without running any cells manually.
Change one follow-up value in a temporary copy of the CSV and list every output that updates.
Restore the source data and render again.


4.13.1 Checkpoint
You can explain the difference between eval, echo, output, and include; identify which cell creates every object; and trace a reported value back to the source data and code that generated it.

title: 5  Research publishing
text:
5.1 Different kinds of research writing
Quarto is not one document style. It is a publishing system that can apply different output conventions to the same structured source.
The underlying Markdown and computation skills transfer across several products:
These are not merely different file extensions. They have different reading conditions. A slide supports a speaker; a manuscript must stand alone. A tutorial asks the reader to act; a report may prioritise a conclusion.
The reusable part is the structured content and analysis. The narrative should still be adapted to its audience.

title: 5  Research publishing
text:
Product
Typical reader
Important features




Analysis note
Yourself or close collaborators
Visible code, diagnostics, rapid iteration


Research report
Client, team, or decision maker
Navigation, executive summary, branded output


Journal manuscript
Editors, reviewers, scholarly readers
Author metadata, citations, numbered objects, submission template


Reproducible manuscript site
Scholarly readers and auditors
Article plus linked computational notebooks and resources


Book or technical manual
Learners and long-form readers
Chapters, navigation, cross-chapter references, search


Teaching practical
Students and instructors
Exercises, starter code, controlled solutions


Presentation
Live audience
Large text, staged explanation, speaker notes

title: 5  Research publishing
section: 5.2 What the outputs actually look like
text:
5.2 What the outputs actually look like
The completed workshop project renders one small analysis to several products.


5.2.1 HTML manuscript



HTML manuscript showing a navigable Results section, folded code, a generated table, and a generated figure.


HTML provides navigation, links, responsive layout, and optional folded code.


5.2.2 Standard PDF manuscript



First page of the standard PDF manuscript with a conventional title block and fixed page layout.


PDF fixes typography and page boundaries for distribution and review.




5.2.3 Elsevier-format PDF



First page of the same demonstration analysis rendered with the bundled Elsevier journal format.


The journal format changes title metadata, typography, citations, and layout.


5.2.4 RevealJS presentation



RevealJS slide showing the same computed sample size and figure in presentation layout.


The result is reused, but the prose is shortened and the visual is enlarged for a live audience.

title: 5  Research publishing
section: 5.3 One source with common and format-specific options
text:
5.3 One source with common and format-specific options
The manuscript declares both HTML and PDF:
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    code-fold: true
    number-sections: true
  pdf:
    number-sections: true
    keep-tex: true
Options indented under html affect only HTML. Options indented under pdf affect only PDF. Shared document metadata sits above format:
title: "Change scores in a synthetic training study"
author: "A. Researcher"
bibliography: bibliography.bib
number-sections: true
format:
  html:
    toc: true
  pdf: default
Move an option to the shared level only when it is valid and intended for every format.
Render one target:
quarto render manuscript.qmd --to html
quarto render manuscript.qmd --to pdf
Render all declared targets:
quarto render manuscript.qmd

Feature
HTML

Word output can be useful even when PDF is the final target. A journal or co-author may require tracked changes in DOCX. Quarto can use a reference DOCX to map semantic elements to organisational styles.
Do not promise that every advanced HTML widget or LaTeX command will transfer perfectly to Word. Prefer portable Markdown, figures, tables, equations, and cross-references when multi-format output matters.

title: 5  Research publishing
text:
5.6 Numbering and cross-references survive reformatting
The section labels introduced in Section 3.4 are format-independent:
## Methods {#sec-methods}

See @sec-methods for the study design.
Figures and tables use the same model:
#| label: fig-primary-result
#| fig-cap: "Primary outcome by study group."
The primary comparison is shown in @fig-primary-result.
The format decides whether the result is “Figure 1”, “Fig. 1”, or another publisher convention. The source refers to a stable identifier rather than a typed number.

title: 5  Research publishing
5  Research publishing
text:
5.8 Author and affiliation metadata
Quarto supports structured authors:
author:
  - name: Alex Researcher
    orcid: 0000-0000-0000-0000
    email: alex@example.edu
    affiliations:
      - ref: university
affiliations:
  - id: university
    name: Example University
    department: School of Research
Structured metadata lets a format decide how names, affiliations, email addresses, and ORCID identifiers appear. A hand-typed title-page paragraph is harder for templates and indexing systems to interpret.

title: 5  Research publishing
5  Research publishing
section: 5.10 Starting a journal article versus adding a format
text:
5.10 Starting a journal article versus adding a format
For a new article based on a supplied template:
quarto use template quarto-journals/elsevier
This creates a project with example metadata and source.
For an existing article:
quarto add quarto-journals/elsevier
This installs the extension under _extensions. The workshop bundles that folder so the demonstration works without downloading it on the day.
The document can then declare:
format:
  elsevier-pdf:
    keep-tex: true
The keep-tex option is useful when a submission requires generated LaTeX source or when a template error needs diagnosis.

title: 5  Research publishing
5  Research publishing
text:
5.12 Conditional content
Occasionally one format needs an explanation or resource that another does not. Quarto supports format-aware content:
::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
Use the navigation panel to explore the analysis.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
The full analysis begins on the next page.
:::
Use conditional content sparingly. Duplicated claims can drift apart. Prefer shared source unless the reading context genuinely differs.

title: 5  Research publishing
section: 5.13 Page and figure problems are diagnostic

title: 5  Research publishing
text:
5.14 Reproducible submission workflow
A defensible workflow is:

Render standard HTML frequently during analysis.
Render PDF regularly rather than only at submission time.
Run a clean render after restarting R.
Inspect every numbered reference and citation.
Render the journal template from the same source.
Compare computed values across outputs.
Read the journal’s current instructions.
Package required source, bibliography, class, figure, and supplementary files.
Preserve the submitted source and environment record.

title: 5  Research publishing
text:
5.15 Publishing exercise
Using manuscript.qmd and journal-demo.qmd:

Render the manuscript to HTML and PDF.
Compare headings, navigation, code display, figures, tables, and references.
Turn section numbering off in HTML only and confirm that cross-references still resolve.
Turn numbering back on.
Render the Elsevier demonstration.
Identify at least five presentation changes and confirm that the sample size and figure data are unchanged.
Find which files in _extensions/quarto-journals/elsevier control the class, bibliography, and title layout.
Write a short submission checklist for a journal relevant to your discipline.


5.15.1 Checkpoint
You can distinguish analysis from format, explain when to start from a template versus add an extension, and verify that multiple outputs remain substantively consistent.

title: 6  Bonus: prove it reruns
text:
6.1 Clean-session check
The final test is not whether the current HTML looks correct. It is whether the project can recreate it from its sources.

title: 6  Bonus: prove it reruns
text:
Save every source file.
Restart R.
Do not run cells interactively.
In the project terminal, run:

quarto render manuscript.qmd

Open the newly rendered outputs.

title: 6  Bonus: prove it reruns
text:
6.2 Reproducibility checklist
Use this checklist before sharing a computational document:

Source data are present and documented.
All paths are relative to the project.
Every reported value is calculated or clearly sourced.
Figures and tables are generated by code.
Labels and cross-references resolve.
Citations and references render.
A fresh R session can render the document.
Required software and packages are listed.
The output contains no private paths, credentials, or unintended data.
Figure descriptions and document structure are accessible.


6.2.1 Final challenge 6 minutes
Without running any R cell manually, rebuild the manuscript. Explain to a neighbour how the sample-size sentence stays synchronised with the CSV.


6.2.2 Workshop outcome
You leave with a functioning literate-programming project containing a manuscript. The project reruns from source and can be used as a reference for your next real document.

title: 6  Bonus: prove it reruns
text:
6.3 Record the environment
The completed manuscript ends with an executable R cell containing:
#| label: session-information
sessionInfo()
This record is useful diagnostic evidence. It is not a dependency lockfile, but it tells a future reader which R and package versions produced the output.

title: 7  Next steps
text:
7.1 Apply the workflow to real work
Choose one modest document rather than migrating an entire research programme. A useful first project has:
Rebuild it as a project with source data, a .qmd file, a bibliography, and a short setup note.

title: 7  Next steps
7  Next steps
section: 7.2 Add safeguards when they solve a problem

title: 7  Next steps
text:
7.3 Keep these habits

Treat rendered documents as products, not the primary source.
Keep inputs immutable and transformations explicit.
Prefer relative paths.
Render from a clean session regularly.
Separate computation from claims: code updates numbers, authors remain responsible for interpretation.
Preserve enough environment information for another person to diagnose a failed rerun.

title: Appendix B — Troubleshooting
text:
B.1 Read the first useful error
Rendering errors often cascade. Start near the first line that names your source file, missing package, missing file, or YAML key.

title: Appendix B — Troubleshooting
text:
B.2 quarto: command not found

Restart the editor or terminal after installing Quarto.
Confirm installation with quarto --version.
On managed university computers, Quarto may need to be installed by IT or selected explicitly in the editor’s preferences.

title: Appendix B — Troubleshooting
section: B.3 An R package is missing
text:
B.3 An R package is missing
Run:
Rscript setup.R
Or install an individual package in R:
install.packages("readr")
Restart R and render again.

title: Appendix B — Troubleshooting
section: B.4 The CSV cannot be found
text:
B.4 The CSV cannot be found

Confirm the terminal is inside the extracted project folder.
Confirm data/training-study.csv exists.
Use the relative path exactly as written, including letter case.
Do not use setwd() to conceal a project-location problem.

title: Appendix B — Troubleshooting
Appendix B — Troubleshooting
text:
B.6 PDF will not render

Confirm HTML works:
quarto render manuscript.qmd --to html
Check for a LaTeX engine:
quarto check latex
If none is found, install TinyTeX in R:
install.packages("tinytex")
tinytex::install_tinytex()
Restart the editor and rerun Rscript preflight.R.

If a managed computer blocks installation, continue with HTML and use the provided completed PDF during the format-comparison activity.

title: Appendix B — Troubleshooting
text:
B.7 A figure reference shows ?

Give the producing cell a unique label beginning with fig-.
Add fig-cap.
Refer to the label as @fig-name.
Render the entire document again.

For tables, use a tbl- label and tbl-cap.

title: Appendix B — Troubleshooting
section: B.8 It worked interactively but not when rendered
text:
B.8 It worked interactively but not when rendered
The interactive R session contained an object or package that the document did not create or load. Restart R and add the missing setup to the .qmd source. This is a useful reproducibility failure, not a reason to avoid clean sessions.

title: Appendix B — Troubleshooting
Appendix C — Python and Jupyter translation
text:
C.1 Preflight
The live workshop uses R so the room can share one execution path. Quarto also supports Python through Jupyter.
Check Python and Jupyter:
Create an environment using your organisation’s preferred tool, then install:
Environment creation and dependency locking differ among venv, Conda, Poetry, and uv; follow local policy rather than mixing them casually.

title: Appendix C — Python and Jupyter translation
text:
python --version
quarto check jupyter

python -m pip install jupyter pandas matplotlib

title: Appendix C — Python and Jupyter translation
text:
C.2 Python cell
In an executable Python cell, write:
#| label: load-data-python

import pandas as pd

study = pd.read_csv("data/training-study.csv")
study["change"] = study["followup_score"] - study["baseline_score"]
A .qmd file containing Python cells uses the Jupyter engine unless another engine is selected explicitly.

title: Appendix C — Python and Jupyter translation
text:
C.3 Inline Python
Type the following sentence (the backticks are part of the source):
The study contains `{python} len(study)` participants.

title: Appendix C — Python and Jupyter translation
text:
C.4 Figure
#| label: fig-change-python
#| fig-cap: "Change score by training hours and study group."
#| fig-alt: "Scatterplot of training hours against change score."

title: Appendix C — Python and Jupyter translation
text:
C.5 Concepts that transfer directly

Markdown and YAML
relative paths
source/output separation
cell labels and most presentation options
citations and cross-references
HTML, PDF, and RevealJS formats
clean-session rendering

The main differences are environment management, package APIs, and the computational engine.

title: Appendix D — Accessibility checklist
text:
D.1 Structure
Reproducible output should also be usable output.

title: Appendix D — Accessibility checklist
text:
Use headings in order; do not choose levels for visual size.
Use real lists and tables rather than spaces or manual line breaks.
Give links descriptive text rather than “click here”.
State the document language.

title: Appendix D — Accessibility checklist
text:
D.2 Figures
Every meaningful figure should have fig-alt that describes:

the chart type;
the variables and comparison;
the major visible pattern; and
information not already supplied by the caption.

Do not begin with “image of”. Decorative images should have empty alt text.

title: Appendix D — Accessibility checklist
text:
D.3 Colour

Do not encode groups by colour alone; add shape, labels, or direct annotation where practical.
Use palettes with adequate contrast.
Check figures in greyscale.
Avoid red/green as the only distinction.

title: Appendix D — Accessibility checklist
text:
D.4 Tables and code

Keep tables small and give them captions.
Avoid merged cells where possible.
Wrap long code lines and avoid screenshots of code.
Explain what a code example is intended to demonstrate.

title: Appendix D — Accessibility checklist
text:
D.5 Slides

Use large text and high contrast.
Keep one main idea per slide.
Describe visual material aloud.
Add speaker notes for required descriptions and facilitation cues.
Provide the HTML or PDF afterward so participants can revisit the content.

title: Appendix D — Accessibility checklist
text:
D.6 Final check
Inspect both HTML and PDF. A correct source does not guarantee equivalent accessibility across output formats.

title: Appendix E — Beyond the workshop
text:
E.1 Git
These tools strengthen the workflow but are intentionally outside the live three-hour session.
Git records source changes and supports collaboration. Start by tracking source files, data that may be shared legally, the bibliography, and _extensions. Ignore generated output unless a publishing workflow requires it.
Never commit credentials, confidential data, or files you do not have permission to distribute.

title: Appendix E — Beyond the workshop
text:
E.2 renv
For an R project:
install.packages("renv")
renv::init()
renv::snapshot()
This creates a lockfile describing package versions. Collaborators can use renv::restore(). Review organisational policy before committing package archives or configuring private repositories.

title: Appendix E — Beyond the workshop
text:
E.3 Automated rendering
A continuous-integration job can:

restore dependencies;
run quarto render;
fail when code or references break; and
publish validated static output.

Automation is most useful after the project renders reliably on a clean local session.

title: Appendix E — Beyond the workshop
text:
E.4 Quarto manuscripts
Quarto manuscript projects connect an article, computational notebooks, and multiple output formats. They are useful when the computational record itself is part of the publication.

title: Appendix E — Beyond the workshop
text:
E.5 Parameters and profiles
Parameters can create repeated reports for different cohorts or datasets. Profiles can change configuration for student, solution, draft, and production builds. Prefer these mechanisms once repeated manual switches are causing real errors.
